_comment: Registration for scripts/bandit-audit.py (issue #962).
WHY THIS GATE NEEDS A COMMITTED CASE (ADR 0008): it is a gate that lets work
THROUGH. `make verify` and the CI `bandit-audit` step read its green as 'no
unaccounted MEDIUM+ security finding in lib/ or scripts/', and nothing
downstream re-derives that. Issue #962 asks for the control by name and names
the way it gets built blind: 'pick a fixture triggering a skipped check and it
goes green while the gate is doing nothing, which is indistinguishable from a
working gate. Confirm the fixture's rule ID is outside the skip list, and say
so.'
SAID SO, IN BOTH PLACES IT HAS TO BE SAID. This gate carries NO skip list at
all - that is #962's decision - so the list a fixture must be outside of is
the one that REPLACED it, `.bandit-audit-allow`. A control whose fixture is
covered by the very mechanism under test proves nothing.
THAT IS NOT A HYPOTHETICAL, AND IT IS WHY THE CASE PATHS ARE FIXTURES. The
first cut of these cases named `lib/cicd/steps.py` B602 - a real file, and
one this repository's own allowlist accepts - so the known-bad case would
have been SUPPRESSED the moment anyone ran the gate against it with the
default `--allow-file` rather than the case's own. It passed here only
because the invocation below points at the case's ledger. The paths are now
`lib/fixture/*` and `scripts/fixture-*`, which exist nowhere, and
tests/test_bandit_audit.py pins the property against the real allowlist
instead of leaving it to this comment. The live selftest fixture is checked
the same way: its rule must be on neither list, asserted against bandit's
own report rather than read off a docstring.
THE ANCHOR IS CxPP's OWN ONE-LINER, NOT A STRAWMAN. `bandit -r lib scripts -ll
--quiet --skip B104,B108,B310,B602` is what codex-power-pack runs today and
what #962 exists to reject; the anchor is a faithful implementation of it.
That makes the demonstration BE the issue's thesis rather than an illustration
of it: measured on CPP's tree at adoption, that skip list removes 10 of 11
MEDIUM+ findings. Each bad case below is one thing the one-liner structurally
cannot see.
THE CASES REPLAY COMMITTED CAPTURES, NOT LIVE SCANS, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN
DECISION HERE. The `negative-controls` CI step runs a bare `python3` with no
`uv sync`, so the bandit binary is absent there; a control whose invocation
needed it would report UNSIGNALLED - an environment failure wearing the
diagnosis 'the gate stopped discriminating', which is the exact collapse this
harness's verdict vocabulary exists to prevent, and which it has no word for.
So each case is a capture of bandit's own JSON plus a fixture allowlist:
stdlib-only, offline, needing no binary and no network, and therefore valid in
BOTH environments that run this harness - the negative-controls step AND
`validate`'s pytest - per ADR 0008's clause 'a control must be valid WHERE THE
HARNESS RUNS'. The precedents are controls/dependency-audit, which replays
pip-audit captures, and controls/check-oscillation, which replays `git log`
because git is absent from the CI image.
WHAT THESE CASES DO NOT ESTABLISH, SAID PLAINLY: that bandit is invoked at
all, or invoked against the files we meant. A capture is replayed, not
produced. That half is covered by `bandit-audit.py --selftest`, which scans
two committed fixture trees live - controls/bandit-audit/live/, one holding a
B307 `eval` it must report and one clean it must not - and which the CI step
runs BEFORE the real audit, so no clean verdict is issued by a scan that was
never shown able to find something. Neither half is sufficient alone; naming
which one covers which is the point.
SEVEN CASES, because the gate draws five distinctions and a control that
exercises one leaves the others unproven:
bad-unaccounted-shell    a B602 nothing accounts for - the case issue #962
requires committed, and the one the inherited skip
list makes invisible.
bad-stale-allowlist      a suppression that suppresses NOTHING. The reverse
direction, and the one that keeps the residual
honest: without it a line outlives the finding it
records and becomes a permanent blindfold nobody
re-reads. A `--skip` has no such direction at all.
bad-inline-nosec         the ledger's BYPASS. A bare `# nosec` deletes a finding
from the report before the gate sees it - measured
directly, a `# nosec` on a shell=True line removed
its B602 entirely - so an allowlist that is tracked,
counted and printed can sit beside an untracked,
uncounted, unprinted one in the source.
bad-unreviewed-low-rule  the band BELOW the threshold, added by #1114. A LOW
finding gates nothing by severity and never will -
that is #962's threshold decision and it is
untouched. What this case exercises is a different
question the count alone could not hold: is this rule
class one somebody READ, or one nobody has looked at?
An eighth class arriving and a fifty-eighth finding of
the first move the same integer by one. Its pair,
good-reviewed-low-rule, replays the SAME capture and
differs only by the reviewed-low record, so the verdict
can only have come from that record - and it carries a
record matching NOTHING while still expecting GOOD,
which pins the deliberate asymmetry with the stale
`finding` record above.
bad-rule-scoped-nosec    the ledger's OTHER bypass, in the field the first
cut read for the wrong thing. `# nosec B307`
increments `skipped_tests` and leaves `nosec` at 0,
so a gate reading only `nosec` misses the form a
careful author is MORE likely to write.
THIS CASE REPLACED ONE THAT WAS WRONG, and the replacement is recorded rather
than quietly swapped. `bad-skip-list-present` declared `skipped_tests=4` on the
belief that the field counts a `--skip` reaching the tool. Measured on bandit
1.9.4 it does not: `--skip B307` yields `skipped_tests=0` and simply omits the
finding. The case therefore modelled a report bandit never emits - a fixture
built to the author's belief rather than to the tool, which is this directory's
own failure class occurring inside it, and it was found by the counter-model
review rather than by the author. The CLI-flag question moved to where it can
actually fail: `BANDIT_FLAGS` is ONE list shared by the audit and by
`--selftest`, so a suppression flag added to it stops the live fixture
reporting and reddens the run before the audit, and tests/test_bandit_audit.py
asserts the constructed argv and the build files carry no such flag.
The GOOD case exercises the COUNT rather than only the (file, rule) pair: two
B602 findings in one file against a line accepting exactly two. A gate matching
on the pair alone passes that case too, so the count is what makes a THIRD
shell=True in that file a finding rather than a silent inheritance. THE HALF
THAT MATTERS for a gate wedged at 'fail': a check that refuses every input is
indistinguishable from a working one on the bad cases alone, and this gate
reddens CI, so a false red blocks every merge in the repository.

cases.name: bad-unaccounted-shell
cases.why: One B602 in the fixture path lib/fixture/shellout.py and an empty allowlist. If this scores GOOD the gate cannot see an unaccounted MEDIUM+ finding at all, which is the only thing it exists to see. The anchor drops B602 by rule and prints a clean line - the precise blindness issue #962 was filed about, and the reason its skip list was re-decided rather than inherited.

cases.name: bad-stale-allowlist
cases.why: A clean report beside a line accepting one B602 in lib/fixture/shellout.py - the state the tree enters the moment someone FIXES a recorded site. The forward check alone scores that tree clean, so without this case the ledger accumulates lines accounting for nothing and nobody is told. The anchor has no ledger, so it cannot have a stale one.

cases.name: bad-inline-nosec
cases.why: No results, and metrics declaring nosec=1 for lib/fixture/shellout.py - what bandit emits when a `# nosec` comment deleted a finding before the report was written. If this scores GOOD the visible ledger has an invisible twin in the source tree, and ADR 0008's 'suppressions are visible or they do not happen' is unenforced. The anchor never reads the field.

cases.name: bad-rule-scoped-nosec
cases.why: No results, and metrics declaring skipped_tests=1 for lib/fixture/shellout.py - what bandit emits for a RULE-SCOPED `# nosec B307`, which leaves `nosec` at 0. If this scores GOOD, the form of inline suppression a careful author is more likely to write is invisible while the bare form is caught, and the visible ledger has an invisible twin after all. The anchor reads neither field. This case replaced `bad-skip-list-present`, which declared skipped_tests=4 on the incorrect belief that the field counts a CLI `--skip`; see the comment above.

cases.name: bad-unreviewed-low-rule
cases.why: One LOW B110 in the fixture path lib/fixture/hashing.py, against a ledger holding a reviewed-low record for a DIFFERENT class (B404). Issue #1114's mechanism: the LOW band is below the threshold and gates nothing, so before this the gate could count it but could not tell a rule class somebody READ from one nobody has - both are increments of the same integer. If this scores GOOD that distinction does not exist and the seven dispositions in ADR 0010 are a claim nothing re-derives. The ledger deliberately is not empty: an empty one would also score BAD while leaving 'the gate reads this file at all' unproven. The anchor drops everything below MEDIUM by -ll, so it prints a clean line here - the blindness under test, one band down from the one it was built for.

cases.name: good-reviewed-low-rule
cases.why: THE SAME capture as bad-unreviewed-low-rule and the same B404 record, differing only by a reviewed-low B110 line - so the verdict can only have come from that line, which makes the pair a measurement rather than two assertions. It pins the other half too: the B404 record matches nothing here and this case still expects GOOD, because a reviewed-low record accounting for nothing is a NOTE and never a finding. That asymmetry with a STALE `finding` record (which does redden - a suppression outliving its finding is a blindfold) is deliberate, and a gate that reddened on it would redden when somebody deletes the last `import subprocess` in a file, which is how a ledger gets switched off (ADR 0009).

cases.name: good-all-accounted
cases.why: Three findings, all accounted for, with the count exercised: two B602 in one file against a line accepting exactly two, plus one B108. THE HALF THAT MATTERS for a gate wedged at 'fail' - the bad cases alone cannot tell a working gate from one that refuses everything, and this gate reddens CI, so a false red blocks every merge in the repository. Both rules are on CxPP's skip list deliberately: the anchor must AGREE here or it differs for reasons beyond the blindness under test, and it can only agree on findings it drops.

anchors.why: CONSTRUCTED, not historical, and PERMANENTLY so. ADR 0008 pre-ruled this for #962 by name: a gate introduced by its own pull request has no blind ancestor on main, its anchor commit dies with the squash, and `--verify-provenance` will therefore read `unverified` forever rather than 'git is absent here'. Recording the terminal cause here is the ADR's own instruction, so a reader chasing the provenance does not hunt for an object that was never going to exist - integrity is established by the sha256 above, historicity is not. WHAT IT IS: codex-power-pack's live one-liner, `bandit -r lib scripts -ll --quiet --skip B104,B108,B310,B602`, faithfully implemented. Not a strawman - it is the implementation this issue exists to reject, and the one a copy-paste adoption would have landed. It accepts `--allow-file` and ignores it, which is the blindness under test rather than an oversight; it prints `BANDIT-FINDING:` when it does report, so an anchor that unexpectedly CAUGHT a known-bad input scores INERT rather than UNRESOLVED (#946).
